Group Reflection

Group Reflection

Group Reflection

Skills inventory

Functions & refactoring (W2)

What we did:

We created reusable R functions for repetitive tasks such as data cleaning and indicator calculations. We also organised the project into separate scripts to make the workflow easier to maintain.

What worked well:

Using functions reduced duplicated code and made later changes much easier.

What was hard:

It was initially difficult to decide which parts of the code should become reusable functions.

Debugging (W3)

What we did:

We debugged errors related to joins, spatial objects, missing values and inconsistent variable names.

What worked well:

Breaking the code into smaller steps helped identify problems quickly.

What was hard:

Some errors originated from incompatible data types and spatial data structures, which were difficult to locate.

Version control & remotes (W4)

What we did:

We used GitHub to store the project, track changes and collaborate on the analysis.

What worked well:

GitHub provided a reliable backup and allowed us to keep the project organised.

What was hard:

Merge conflicts and keeping files synchronised required attention.

Quarto websites & collaborative coding (W5)

What we did:

We created a Quarto website to present our analysis, maps and conclusions.

What worked well:

Quarto combined code, text and figures into a clear and reproducible report.

What was hard:

Formatting pages and ensuring all links rendered correctly required several revisions.

R packages (W6)

What we did:

We mainly used tidyverse, sf, janitor and ggplot2 for data manipulation, spatial analysis and visualisation.

What worked well:

These packages integrated well and supported our workflow efficiently.

What was hard:

Working with sf objects required additional learning because spatial data behave differently from ordinary data frames.

Initial data analysis & data cleaning (W7)

What we did:

We cleaned multiple datasets, standardised district identifiers and combined population data with public toilet locations.

What worked well:

Cleaning the data early prevented many problems later in the project.

What was hard:

Different datasets used inconsistent variable names and formats, requiring extensive preprocessing.

Reproducibility, open data & renv (W9)

What we did:

We documented our workflow and worked with publicly available datasets so that the analysis could be reproduced.

What worked well:

Using open data increased transparency.

What was hard:

Some external datasets changed over time, making reproducibility more challenging.

Analysis & inference strategies (W10)

What we did:

Instead of comparing the absolute number of toilets, we calculated the number of toilets per 10,000 inhabitants for each district.

What worked well:

Population standardisation provided a fair comparison across districts.

What was hard:

Choosing an appropriate indicator required discussion because several alternatives were possible.

Communication & visualisation (W11)

What we did:

We created choropleth maps, summary tables and explanatory text to communicate our findings.

What worked well:

Maps made regional differences easy to understand.

What was hard:

Balancing visual simplicity with sufficient information required several iterations.

Key analytical decisions

Decision 1: Standardising by population

Instead of comparing the total number of toilets, we calculated toilets per 10,000 inhabitants. This allowed meaningful comparisons between districts of different population sizes.

In hindsight, would we decide differently?

No. This was one of the most important methodological decisions in the project.

Decision 2: Using districts as the unit of analysis

We aggregated toilet locations to Munich districts rather than analysing individual toilets.

This simplified interpretation and allowed us to combine demographic information with spatial data.

In hindsight?

Yes, we would still make this decision.

Decision 3: Combining multiple open datasets

We combined toilet data, district boundaries and population statistics.

Although data integration required significant cleaning, it greatly improved the quality of the analysis.

Workflow & collaboration

How did we divide work across group members?

Tasks were divided between data collection, data cleaning, analysis, visualisation and report writing. Members communicated regularly to integrate their work into a single project.

What branching or Git workflow did we actually use?

We mainly worked through GitHub by committing changes regularly and synchronising the repository. The workflow was simpler than originally planned but sufficient for our project.

What would we change about how we coordinated?

Earlier coordination and more frequent communication would have reduced duplicated work and simplified integration.

LLM usage

Usage 1: Debugging R code

Tool / model

ChatGPT

What it produced

Suggestions for fixing join errors, data wrangling problems and ggplot code.

What we had to correct or verify

We verified every suggestion manually because some variable names and column references did not match our datasets.

Usage 2: Improving explanations

Tool / model

ChatGPT

What it produced

Suggestions for improving the wording of explanations and report sections.

What we had to correct or verify

We checked that all interpretations matched our own results rather than relying on generated text.
